utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Good morning. Your Honour, last Wednesday on the 25th of February, I brought to the Chamber's attention the Milan Lukic Defence team's non-compliance with the Chamber's order of the 27th of January, 2009, to disclose the identifying information of their witnesses. I requested that the Chamber order them to fully comply before the start of court on Thursday the 26th, and the Chamber ordered precisely that at transcript page 4809. The Defence did not comply with that order. Further, our correspondence since that order was issued seeking to remind them of the order has gone ignored. The Milan Lukic Defence has ignored our correspondence, has ignored two direct and clear orders of the Court. I submit this is a very, very important matter. I bear the burden of establishing that these witnesses do not raise a reasonable doubt, a task that is very difficult to discharge when I do not know with any certainty who in fact they are. I now ask the Court to direct the Milan Lukic Defence by the start of the second session this morning to provide the Prosecution with a list of all remaining witnesses with the biographical information ordered by the Court. If they fail to comply, I ask the Chamber not to allow them to call any additional witnesses until they have complied with the Chamber's previous orders. It undermines the integrity of this trial to proceed in the face of the Defence's utter disregard of its procedural obligations and its flagrant failure to abide by clear directives of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, this relates to what particular witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have not received the dates of birth, the father's name, the mother's name, the place of birth of many of the remaining Defence witnesses. I need that information to do some investigation, to make requests of governments with respect to whether these people have any criminal convictions. All of that takes some time, and as I said last week, Your Honour, as yet I've not yet had to ask the Chamber to defer cross-examination, but I fear the time is coming when I will not have heard back or will not have the results of any of our investigative efforts. I will be asking the Chamber to postpone the cross-examination until we can complete it. This is information that we should have had prior to the start of the Defence case. We are now about midway through the Defence case, and we still have not been provided this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what you want would be the dates of birth of the witnesses, the father's name, the mother's name, the place of birth. Mr. Alarid, why haven't you provided that? It seems to me to be a monumental task.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with some witnesses it has been, and we have given the Prosecution all information within our control. Accordingly, people that we're not able to get confirmation on, these sort of tangential witnesses that were out there and possibility, we've not gotten, so -- our remedy would be not to call them because, of course, if we don't have the control or ability to get this simple information and kind of cooperation, then they probably wouldn't be a very good witness for this court. So, grand scheme of things, that may affect the number of witnesses we ultimately present, but I cannot give what I do not have the ability to get through other means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So your basic response is that you have given the Prosecution all that you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, he has given you all that he has.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems to me -- I mean, they are witnesses that the Defence intends to call. I mean, they've interviewed these people. Why were these questions not asked of these people when they were interviewed? It's a basic obligation. If Mr. Alarid is saying now that he may decide not to call some of these witnesses, then I think I'm also entitled to know that because I have people assigned to be -- that are presently working on the statements, on the witness list that's been provided by the Defence. Mr. Alarid knows now that he's not going to call them. Why waste our time with this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, have you decided that you will not call these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm on the verge. I mean, I can't delay the Court. I can't necessarily get things, especially from the distance of the Balkans. That is a problem. There are witnesses we had never interviewed. That is Mr. Groome's point, but that's also been my point this entire time. And along those lines, Your Honour, we did make a filing this morning, though, that I think gives the impetus of the Court -- of the information the Court wanted as to why the investigator of the OTP would further -- add further to the court proceedings, and we'll be asking for that, and namely we filed our notice of surviving victims that we have located and that we have found, and I've personally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In respect of the witnesses that you have interviewed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- have you provided that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because you really ought to have gotten that information, and in respect --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We've provided everyone that we intend to call, Your Honour. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In respect of the witnesses you have not yet interviewed, I understand you to be saying that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yeah, the only ones that we would not be able to provide, and it's also based on our response, was the pending subpoenas. You know, there's police officer that needs to come per a subpoena and so forth. We don't have the ability, really, to interview, nor would that really be in the nature of what we would get in anticipation of trial. So the subpoena is outstanding. We wouldn't be able to get those, i.e., Risto Perisic, Branimir Savovic. To be honest, I mean, I guess we could do some research on Google to find that out, but that would be the extent of my ability to find that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that may be what you have to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, rather than leave it at this kind of vague, well, there are some witnesses that won't be called, could I ask then that the Chamber direct Mr. Alarid to inform us in written form what witnesses have been previously noticed that he now knows he will not be calling so that I can cease work that's being done in preparation for those witnesses. It seems like a basic courtesy, but if it requires a court order, I would ask for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll do that. Mr. Alarid, in respect of the witnesses that you have previously noticed, inform the Prosecution which of those witnesses you will not be calling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us move to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This has been reviewed by my Chamber, and the view is that the evidence is very sparse. What I would do is when the witness comes in, I will question the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to be heard, though --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: -- before the witness comes in just because there's some major points that need to be made. First of all, on the face of the motion it's unclear what they are asking for. In one paragraph, they are asking for name identity redaction only, but then at the end when they ask for the relief, they're asking for a face and voice distortion; so, number one, it's unclear. Two, this is grossly untimely. This Court has ordered that the Defence has to provide two weeks' notice if they're going to file motions for protective measures, that we have an opportunity to investigate and respond. They have known about this witness since the very beginning. He has been on his list since the beginning. They filed an amended 65 ter summary in January, so presumably they had spoken with the witness then in order to file an amended summary. Moreover, this witness has been here for probably close to a week, and they have never indicated in any way, shape, or form that this witness wanted protective measures. Now they come in on the eve of trial and ask for protective measures, and I won't go into the real and objective standard that Your Honour has articulated in previous decisions, but it's our position that they have not met that burden. For instance, they say that the witness is fearful,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems to me that his former membership must be a factor. It would draw attention to himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, every witness who comes in here, Your Honour, has attention drawn to himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: (redacted) And furthermore, drawing attention to one's self, that's going to happen with any witness who walks in here and testifies, whether he has had any type of threats, any type of -- any reason to believe that drawing attention to himself is going to cause any harm to himself or his family, and he hasn't articulated that, (redacted) I'm this, I'm that. It doesn't -- he hasn't articulated it under the standard that is required to get protective measures in this court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: (redacted) All witnesses in these cases have a certain amount of fear and apprehension, but in order to be granted protective measures which prevents the public and other witnesses from hearing this person's testimony, there has to be a particular, articulable, measurable, objective fear, and we just don't have that here. Again, they've raised the issue of the Bakira Hasecic. This Court has already refused to acknowledge that that has any merit. Her demonstrations or what-not have no merit to claim for protective measures. So we would agree, and again, I wanted to put on the record the timeliness issue as well as our argument that where we agree that the evidence is very scant, and unless the witness can articulate a specific fear, then we would request that the protective measures be denied.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: (redacted) the protection of his colleagues and former colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear from Mr. Alarid in response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I mean, I think the initial threat to the sanctity of the testimony is the horrible tabloidesque media coverage that this case gets in Bosnia specifically. And so we can anticipate that the information of this gentleman would be blasted across Bosnia the minute that this court session ends. So that is a foregone conclusion. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's possible, but it hasn't been articulated by the Defence. I mean, as of Friday when this witness was scheduled to testify, he needed no protective measures. Now over the course of the weekend, I mean, I'm interested in learning what has happened over the weekend that has now caused him to have concern for his safety. One of the things mentioned in both applications is that a Defence witness has been named -- a protected Defence witness has been named in the Bosnian press. I think that's a very serious matter. I would ask Mr. Alarid to please specify or provide for the Court and for the Prosecution the actual newspaper article where a protected Defence witness was -- the name was -- the identity was compromised and divulged. That's somewhat not directly related to what we're talking about now, but I do note that the Prosecution certainly takes it very serious that anyone would violate a protective measure of the Chamber and would support any effort to investigate the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us just deal with the application that is before us. I'm going to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. On the basis of the submissions that have been made, the Chamber will grant the witness's pseudonym, but not face and voice distortion. Let the witness be called. Mr. Alarid, in respect of the order that I made earlier that you are to provide the Prosecution with a list of the witnesses that you are not calling, I will further order that that be done by the end of this week. That's Friday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, may we go into private session for the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, before we get into the background information with regards to this, when were you first contacted and by whom for the Milan Lukic Defence in hopes of you testifying here in court today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: It must have been in December, anyway, before new year, in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And who did you meet with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: With Danny.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But with regards to the nature of your testimony, did we meet here in The Hague on a couple of occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you please state for the record your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And without revealing the exact location of your address, could you tell us what municipality you live in?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could you also tell us where you lived in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you serve your compulsory military service with people of other ethnicities and religions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How did you get along with other people of other ethnicities and religions in the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: We got a long excellently. I had a friend from Zagreb. We were inseparable. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in 1992, where were you when the -- when you first remember hostilities beginning in and around Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I was in my village of Gornja Dubova, and we took positions at Panos to protect the Serbian villages, but that's when the war had begun already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, can you tell me, in 1992 were you mobilised into the forces of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, it was kind of -- we organised ourselves in the countryside to protect ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How were you mobilised officially, can you tell us, and when were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, the late Tomic told me to come -- I don't know when it was. The Uzice Corps -- corpus came, the Uzice Corps came, and then I was -- but I don't remember when the -- these summons was actually handed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, you indicate that: "The late Tomic told me to come ..." How did -- tell me who this late Tomic is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: The late Tomic was the commander of the SUP, the public security station at Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you state his full name, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Dragan Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how did he tell you to come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, he had fled to Panos. All the Serbs had left toward the border with Serbia, and I said that I was supposed to go to Uzice to work, but I wasn't sure what would happen, whether they would really hire me, and he said to me, Doesn't matter, you will always have work here, I'll give you a job. When the Uzice Corps came, he went to town and invited me to come and see him, and that's when I joined the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And as you joined the reserve police force, tell me how that came about. What did they do to make it official?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, he told me to be shaven and to turn up at 7.00 in the morning, and that was that. It was on the day when we met. It was around noon, and he said to me that I should come again at 7 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you returned, were you given a uniform? Were you issued any equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yeah, we did get a uniform, but it wasn't much. It was a very greenish colour. It was -- it had some stripes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were you immediately given a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes, on that day. Actually, on the following day when I returned, I got my uniform around noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could you explain for the court, please, the functioning and structure of the reserve police in Visegrad at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: It was organised like the army. There were check-points. We would be at Brodar for ten days without relief, and we went wherever we were ordered to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what kind of instructions or training did Commander Tomic give you on how to do your job as a reserve police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. There wasn't any kind of training, really. No training. They send you to some place to be on watch, or we would spend seven days in a wood as recon or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I might have asked you this already, but how old were you at this time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Around 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how did it make you feel at this time being in the reserve police officer corps? Did you feel that you could lose your life in this role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And can you tell us what other kind of uniforms the reserve misused during your time in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: We also had camouflage uniforms, but they were not necessarily all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And why not? Why weren't they all the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, sometimes we would get 20 uniforms at a time, and then there would be another batch, and they would not be exactly the same. Most of them were camouflage uniforms, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did any of the soldiers actually procure their own uniforms because of the shortfalls that were official?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Even I got a uniform from Serbia. Toward the end of the war, a friend sent me that uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, what kinds of badges or emblems were you issued upon being mobilised to the police of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I am not sure at what time that was. There was a ribbon which read "milicija."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And of these patches -- or was it a patch or an emblem? You said ribbon, but that may be the translation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: It was -- it was sewed upon our uniform, and I took it to my sister-in-law to do that for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Are you saying that it was your responsibility to sew on your own patches and emblems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And ultimately how many uniforms did you have in all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I had several, four or five, maybe. Not of that kind; they were different. But they were very similar, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with regards to official emblems or patches, were there always enough for everyone within the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think this calls for speculation. Whether this man was in charge of handing out patches, I believe he should lay some type of foundation before asking this broad question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid. Lay a foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: MLD23, did you have an understanding as to the availability of official patches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. The availability of patches?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were there enough patches to go around for all the reservists, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Again, this calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: As far as he knows, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Do you know whether there were enough patches, Witness, for all the reservists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's your answer? That most probably not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure there were not enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us again about the first uniforms that were worn by the Visegrad police. What colour were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: The first uniforms were camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were there any blue uniforms issued to anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: For sure, until they were able to procure camouflage uniform, but those were more like firefighters' suits. They weren't any good for -- but whoever already had a camouflage uniform was allowed to wear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What about any hats? Were there any official hats at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yeah, we got blue berets, but we only wore it for a short while because when they got wet, they would shrink and you could no longer wear them. So we wore them only for a very short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And as a reserve police officer, were you required to go into combat situations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how were these blue hats -- how would they effect you being in combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: No. In no way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, would there be occasions where full-time legitimate members of the law enforcement of the police of Visegrad would have different uniforms from one another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Could you repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it be uncommon for various members of the law enforcement of the police of Visegrad to have different uniforms from one another?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So far as you observed, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: No, they did not wear different uniforms. You mean as if we were divided into groups so that one group would wear one kind of uniform and another group a different kind of uniform? I'm not quite clear what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No, I mean just people using whatever uniform they had available.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is a leading question, and, again, it's very broad. He can ask the witness what he saw but not this kind of question. It's speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You do appear to be leading, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'll try not to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would there be occasion where people of the same group would simply wear different uniforms that they had available to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you were mobilised, what kind of weapon were you issued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: At first, an automatic rifle. Sorry, semi-automatic rifle, the long one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was there any point in time where you were issued a different one, a different rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Automatic rifle with a folding stock.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of automatic rifle, the model or make?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I've forgotten. I used to know, but I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you may have touched on this a little bit, but what kind of specific duties made up your official duties as a reservist assigned to the police in Visegrad in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, sometimes I would stand guard for one stint outside the SUP in Visegrad, or I would work at the check-point or anywhere they sent me, or I was told to go and hand call-up papers to someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would you consider this an ordinary day, or what would an ordinary day be like in your service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, maybe fighting would cause casualties. Somewhere somebody would be killed. We would be sent to pull them out or pick up the bodies. You never knew what duty you would be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, what kind of threats did you endure on a daily basis from what you considered the enemy forces at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: All kinds of threats. The moment you got into the car and travelled on the road, you could die. You could get killed. You could step on a mine. We moved everywhere, walked through the woods anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that was going to be my next question as to how you got around normally between your various assignments and duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, when you were given orders, you had to go wherever you were sent. We would sometimes pass through a minefield and then discover it only on the way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in terms -- you said that sometimes you would be in a car. What kind of cars did you use as part of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: All kinds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you have any official vehicles in the police force at that time, official marked police units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Two cars, perhaps, maybe three service cars, but service cars were later taken away and taken to Gorazde or Sarajevo - I don't know - when the Muslims took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Explain that a little more. What cars were taken away, and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: When they were withdrawing towards Gorazde, they took with them those service cars, whatever they could get their hands on. Late Vidoje once went to Gorazde and retrieved one of these cars, and one was later found somewhere outside a place called Moremiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We'll get to Vidoje in a second, but did you ever receive any written instructions from the police station or police commanders about what you were to do on a given day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How did the commanders tell you what to do on a given day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, we would be put on a list for a certain duty, depending on who the leader was. If we were going into action, there would be one of us appointed as the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was the worst assignment you had during the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, where is this evidence taking us to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's our position that Mr. Lukic was part of the reserve police force when initially mobilised. This is to give you a picture considering he is the only police officer that we've brought as to give the Court a picture as to what the structure was, the ordinary duties, as we've not presented any testimony prior to this day. He is the one witness we are bringing in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio, are you challenging the fact that Mr. Lukic was a part of the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are? You are challenging that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thanks. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I think I asked you, what was your worst assignment as a reserve police officer during the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Alarid, is this evidence helping to establish that he was?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just from a foundation perspective, I think it gives the Court the vantage point of seeing that the duties of a reserve officer blurred with those of a regular foot soldier and back and forth again, and I think that's really what I'm trying to establish. If that's -- if I've already made that point, Your Honour, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Move on or made the point, or both?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not answering the question whether you made a point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I would object to Mr. Alarid speaking on the record about what he believes his evidence is in front of the witness especially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's inevitable, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I think it's suggesting answers to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you recall your worst day in the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: My worst day, perhaps, was when we were pulling out the dead, those first two or three victims from Medjedja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell the Court a little bit, and I know it may be difficult, but tell the Court a little bit about those kind of duties.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: We had been for five or six days up there at Donja Lijeska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, I'm having some difficulty. I understand that you want to establish that Mr. Lukic was a member of the reserve force, and this witness, as I understand it, is to tell us something about the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But what does all this have to do? I mean, what is it -- now you are having him telling us about his worst day. What's the importance of his worst day?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how the Court chooses to assess the credibility of a witness, but there comes a point in time where I think that the Court needs certain details about a man and what he does in order to make that assessment. If I've completed that, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want to hear about his worst day. Speak to another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How did your duties as a reserve police officer compare had you been a reserve soldier in the army or member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: First, ask him if he knows about the duties of a member of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I could ask him this, Your Honour:

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: MLD23, were you ever mobilised into the regular army as opposed to being a reserve police officer, or did you stay there the entire time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I was mobilised into the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when were you mobilised into the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: 1993. Towards the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what were you mobilised into the army to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I drove a Praga vehicle. I actually charged the weapon, although my military specialty is driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how did the duties of the reserve police compare to the duties of the army members that you were serving with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection. Your Honour, I think that the question -- he could ask his duties but not just duties in general. I don't believe that a proper foundation has been laid for such a broad speculative question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He has had experience in both.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's my point. He can ask about his experience, but he is asking about everyone's experience, and I don't think that enough foundation has been laid if he wants to ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm trying to get done here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just ask him about his experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How did your experiences in the army compare with your experiences and duties with the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: A reserve policeman went to the battle-field just as soldiers. We could spend ten days in a stint on an elevation or maybe a link-up with one another if it was a longer front-line. We differed in no way from soldiers. We had to go anywhere they sent us. We couldn't refuse orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you were mobilised by Commander Tomic, did you learn of other persons similarly recruited by him such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What kind of [microphone not activated] ... being mobilised by Commander Tomic in this manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: He was looking for younger men, able-bodied, hard-working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: A little bit earlier in the examination, you mentioned a Vidoje. Who is Vidoje, and what's his last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Vidoje Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how do you know Vidoje Andric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: He was our commander, our commanding officer. He led us in action. He would take over from Tomic. He would take orders, and he would say 15 of us are going to some hill or elevation. We would be issued with weapons and ammunition. We would appoint a team of scouts, flanks. We would decide on the formation, but he -- in any case, he was the leader, not all the time but most of the time. He was the second man next to Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how would you describe Vidoje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: He was good man, a brave fighter, indomitable. He had no fear. He was quite able, capable of running into enemy lines, and he was a very strong man. He had no fear at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was Vidoje's calling before the war started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I don't know. I know he worked in the Varda company. He was an athlete. He did Karate, had a black belt, but just before the war I think he was out of work. But I'm not sure about his training.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you know in what manner Vidoje was mobilised when the war started, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I don't know. He was mobilised before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in addition to sometimes commanding your unit, what other kinds of duties did Vidoje Andric have within the Visegrad police?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Again, I don't believe he has laid a foundation how this man knows so much about another person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's either he knows or he doesn't know. Can you tell us what other duties Vidoje had in the Visegrad police? Do you know? We don't want to you speculate. Speak from your knowledge. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vidoje was Tomic's guard. He always accompanied Tomic. He was even appointed as escort once to Velibor Ostojic, but he refused. He stayed where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what other persons were also part of Tomic's guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: There was Vidoje Andric, then Mladen Andric, and Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you said that Vidoje had been recruited as the body-guard for Velibor Ostojic. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: He told me. He said, I can't bear waiting for him in the car when he is sitting somewhere. I hate sitting outside in the car like a dog. It's no job for me. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And who was Velibor Ostojic at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Some sort of minister at Pale. I don't know exactly what.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with regards to Milan Lukic, what was his role in the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: His role in the police was to go out and hand out call-out papers, whatever they told him to do. He was in their entourage. That day they were killed, they had spent the night all together in Okrugla. I know about that because I had left that evening and he stayed, and the next morning those men were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, let's back up a little bit, and you say they were killed. Who was killed and when?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. They are getting into non-noticed -- they're getting into alibi evidence at this point. There's nothing in the witness's 65 ter summary about what I believe this event they're going to get into. There has never been any notice given to us that he is going to testify about that incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, one, that's not true. We're not having him testify as to what I think Ms. Sartorio is implying, and if you'll let me get a little bit more into it, that he was just about to answer, I think you'll understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let's hear the evidence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You say they were killed. Who was they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Dragan Tomic, Vidoje Andric, and Mladen Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How were Tomic and Vidoje and Mladen killed, and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: On the 19th of July at Okrugla. They were driving across a bridge. There had been some wounded up ahead of them where the army lines were, and they were going to pull them out. The road was blocked. There was a log across the road, so they stopped, and there were two mines laid one on top of another. The car was blown up 500 metres in the air. The man Vidoje remained lying in the back seat, and Tomic was still giving signs of life. They took him to the hospital, but he could not survive. The tyre actually got stuck right in the place where the -- where the mine was, and the tyre kept running in place and if that hadn't happened, maybe they would have managed to simply slip by, but they got stuck instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you said a little bit earlier on direct exam that they were together the night before they died. Who is "they," and explain that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: There were a number of troops above the road in those houses, and Milan Lukic was with them for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And where were you that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: The night -- that night we were supposed to move and go around to surround the enemy troops, and we went to an elevation called Granje. There were seven or eight of us. We stayed the night in a man's house, and that morning the action started, there was no resistance. We didn't meet with any resistance, and in the mean time somebody gave us the message that these men had been killed, and we gave up on the action. We went down to Dobra to the police check-point. On the way, we saw the car. The people who are standing around told us who had happened. We were so sorry they had got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, Dragan Tomic was the commander of the Visegrad police at that time to July 19th. Who was the commander after Tomic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I think for 15 days there was no commander. We didn't have a commander. I don't know for how long, until the return of Milan Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And who was the chief of the Visegrad police in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Risto Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what was Dragan Tomic's occupation prior to the outbreak of the war, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: He was commander of the Secretariat for Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court about what type of automobiles were used with the Visegrad police in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: All kinds of cars, some Muslim cars that had been abandoned, some service cars belonging to companies, sometimes a truck, sometimes a Mercedes or a van if there were more of us. It didn't matter. There were all sorts of cars, Lada Nivas, off-road vehicles, civilian cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court why private civilian cars were used and mobilised by the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Because there had not been enough cars. We had nothing to drive. Many cars were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you had told us a story about your own personal vehicle at this time. Can you repeat that to the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I can. I used to have a Lada that my father had bought me. I had left it standing because I had no petrol, and I found it the next time taken apart, all the wires broken. I could not start it, and a man eventually helped me start it, and later on when I went away for 10 to 15 days on stints --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, please stop. Mr. Alarid, I'm getting a little impatient with all of this evidence which doesn't seem to me to be very relevant to the primary purpose for which this witness is here. As I understand it, that purpose is to establish that the accused Milan Lukic was a member of the police reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and Your Honour, the only reason I digressed with that point was because to establish the -- or to refute the Prosecution's theory regarding the civilian vehicles that have been alleged to have been part of the crimes, and I was going to move on after that very question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you moving on to, because, remember, you have brought him here for a specific purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you'll see. I am moving right to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you recall what kinds of cars were the ones used by Commander Dragan Tomic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: He got the better cars. I can't remember specifically. We had no more than two or three white and blue proper police cars. The rest had been taken away. So we had to use Muslim cars that had been requisitioned or company vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Dragan Tomic, did you have occasion to see him in the company of Vidoje Andric and Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with regards to those occasions, when you saw these persons together, how would they be dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Combat fatigues. In camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would you have occasion to see other persons in their company, and can you name any of those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember who else was there. I on occasion was with them in their company.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, with occasion -- this other third -- I'm trying not to lead you, so with regards to any third persons in this company, did you know whether they were members of any organisation or structure within Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: No, they didn't belong to any other organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were they ever in the company of members of the police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I did not understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, just in terms of who they associated with, did Tomic, Andric, and Lukic associate with other members of the police force other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, with us, who else would they socialise with?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think you are correct. We'll take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With the Court's assistance, we would like to call up 65 ter number 5 1D 21-0482.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you -- the copy is not of the best quality, but can you recognise what is on the screen in front of you with the pictures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Fallen soldiers, soldiers fallen in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you have an understanding as to where this book is from and kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, looking at the first page of the book, do you recognise any soldiers, or, excuse me, police officers on this list as being killed? You may have to pan down. Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I know Vidoje Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with the Court's assistance, could we get a marker to mark the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could please circle the person you know as Vidoje Andric.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is there anyone else -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I know Dusko Andric as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Will you please circle Dusko.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Anyone else from this -- what you are able to see on the screen in front of you? Who else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Do you mean who in the police or whether I knew anyone? Should I encircle all of those I knew?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You have a blue pen with you, and let's circle anyone that's in the police in blue first. And if we scroll down, do we lose the -- okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I don't know anybody else, only those two. I know some other people, but I'm not sure whether they were in police. Maybe they were for ten days, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, please put a VA for Vidoje Andric next to his photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And if you could, please circle anyone else that you do know on this page and how you know them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Mico Indzic [phoen] was the first victim. He was killed at Glavica. Then Dragan Filipovic, I know him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, with regards to Vidoje Andric, is his date of death and information correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I apologise, I interrupted you. You were circling other names and telling the court of your knowledge of them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, I was in the action that aimed at retrieving their bodies. Dusko Andric, he was a relative. Then another Andric had been killed 40 days before. I took part in both actions to retrieve the bodies. I spent a night at the -- during the second action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, could the court assistant please just scroll down to see the photos, and save this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And before we move on, right next to Vidoje Andric, who is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: To his right, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, to the right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: That would be Vlatko Trifkovic. He -- killed at the beginning of the war. He was burnt in a car at a bend towards -- I heard they were ambushed. They were all killed. Their bodies were burnt in the car, and some soldiers tried to put the fire out with bottles of water.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, looking at the date --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, looking at the date of death, is that your understanding of when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I can't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could we, with the Court assistance, circle Mr. Trifkovic before we save and move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to circle him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, please. One second.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do we have to re-circle Vidoje Andric? We saved it? Okay. And could we save this page, as well, and move to the next page, and we would introduce this page into evidence with both writings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, this is a document that Mr. Cole attempted to introduce in evidence last week, and it was objected to by Mr. Alarid as there being no lack of foundation or authenticity of the document. So we'll note that for the record, and we have no objection to its admittance if we are able to then call it up on cross-examination and question the witness about other entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, of course, my objection on that day, Your Honour, was lack of foundation through that witness had been improperly established. I would argue that we've established sufficient foundation for him to identify the photographs and mark the exhibit, and we have no objection to calling it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first version will become Exhibit 1D 115, and the second, 1D 116, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, sir, this is at the bottom of that page because we couldn't see it all as we zoomed on the document. Do you recognise anyone at the bottom of this page before we move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D 117.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this is the next page in the book, and with what you can see on the screen, we'd ask you with that same pen to mark anyone that you know and explain to the Court as you are marking how you know them and were they in the police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Pero Kovacevic was not in the police, but he was killed at Moremiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay, and anyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Let me take a look at the others. The photograph is not of high quality. Miodrag Mucelja, I was there where he got killed between Pijevica and Drinsko. We have the same birth year, and we knew each other from school, before the war, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Anyone else before we move on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Let me take a look at the remaining four. This one was killed at Moremiste, as well, by the name of Goran Radjen. It's possible at the very outset, but I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Is that all on this page so we can save and tender it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I know Stevo Draskovic as well. He was killed towards the end of the war. He was ambushed at Kaostice, as it's stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Could we save, and after saving could we tender this marking into evidence and pan down to the lower part of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D 118, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: With these remaining six photographs, was there anyone that you recognise, and were any of them in the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I know this old man. I think he was killed on the bridge. Milan Krsmanovic was his name. Radomir Nikitovic, I think he was killed at Moremiste, but it's stated here that he was killed at Visegrad on the 25th. Maybe I'm mixing him with somebody of the same name, but the one that I knew used to sport a mustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Could we tender this into evidence, and I'd ask the Court for a redaction. Page 41, line 16. The description tends to identify the witness. Specifically states: "He married my mother's sister, and I was at his funeral."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could we then tender this bottom into evidence, as well, and move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D 118, and I understand that Exhibits 1D 115 through 1D 118 have to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And moving on with these pictures on this page, can you identify anyone else, and if so they are in the police, please let the Court know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Jovo Samardzic, he was in police at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And who else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Mladen Andric was in police. He got killed together with Vidoje and Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Anybody else on this page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Allow me a minute to take a look. Slavisa Knezevic, he was from Kragujevac. I know when he was killed, but I am not sure whether he was registered with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Could we -- anyone else before we move on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Radivoje Nikitovic. He was killed at Moremiste. He worked in the military department before the war. He had a rank, but I'm not sure which rank he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could we save and tender this into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D 119 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could we pan down to the bottom of the page to examine the remaining photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And looking at the remaining six photographs on this page, do you recognise anyone else, and if so, please explain whether they were in the police or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: This is Savic, but Mladen or Mladjo, I knew him. He was killed at Moremiste together with Dusko, but he wasn't a member of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we mark and tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is there anyone else on this page before I move?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I don't know. Well, I know this Coric, but I didn't know him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. We'd tender this into evidence and ask that the next page be put on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D 120, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the same questions for this page, if you could locate anyone that you know and tell us whether or not they were in the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And before we move on, I'd like to emphasise number 55 at the upper left-hand corner. Is that true that that says that -- and what's his name again, number 55? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Goran Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And based on your understanding, he died in Kopito, June 20th, 1992; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: That's -- well, I'm not sure when exactly he was killed, most probably since they stated such a date, but I can't recall the date exactly. But I knew him. I knew him well, really well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And with regards to the location of Kopito, referring to the fact that Trifkovic was killed on June 13th in Kopito, was that a hot area or a place of heavy fighting, the Kopito region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes. Fierce fighting, everything across the Drina was a difficult area, up all the way to Sjemec and at Crvenka, people got killed along that road, and we advanced as far as Sjemec, which is Rogatica municipality, and he was -- he hailed from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Before we move on, is there anyone else on this page that you recognise, either 68, 69, or 70?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I don't recognise anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. We'd tender this into evidence and move down to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D 121, Your Honours. Under seal, Your Honours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please review the remaining six photographs and names on this page and tell me who you recognise and whether or not they were in the police or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Dragan Tomic. He was in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please circle Dragan Tomic, and tell the Court for the record what number he is as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: It's number 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And based on your personal knowledge, is the information on this entry correct as to the date and time and place of death?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I think so, certainly for Tomic. Tomic and Andric were killed on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we tender this into evidence and move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D 122, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And please review this page, these 12 photographs, and mark any ones that you recognise as well as indicate whether or not they were in the police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I can't see the first one, and I can't read what it says. I knew this one, but I can't remember everyone who was in the police because we may have been some 200 at the beginning, and then depending on their military training they would be sent elsewhere, so I don't -- such as to drive a tank or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and just to clarify that point, how long were you mobilised in the reserve police before you were re-assigned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: You mean before the war? Before the war, I wasn't with the police at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No, I meant after the war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I was in the reserve forces in 1992 and 1993, and later on I was a soldier in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. Anyone else you recognise on this sheet and whether or not they were in the police, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Milan Simsic, my immediate neighbour from a village, but he wasn't with the police. I was in the village when he was killed. I don't remember the date. It says here the 6th of August. That's certainly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please mark and tender into evidence and move down to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D 123 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please review these last six photographs and tell us whether you know them, and were they in the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I knew this one, Stanimirovic, but I don't remember if he was in the police. Of these people, I only know Stanimirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. We'd please mark and tender into evidence and move to the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D 124 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, this is a little more difficult because there's no photographs to assist you, but let's do the best we can with what we have and see if you can recognise someone or some of the names on this final list and whether or not you knew them to be part of the police, if you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Stanko Pecikoza -- oh, I shouldn't have. No, I won't circle that. Stanko Pecikoza was the founder of the SDS party. Should I circle him? Or the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Certainly. And for the record, that's number 124.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Tosic, Salvo Tosic, he worked at a gas station. He got killed, but I don't remember exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's fine. Anyone else before we tender this into evidence and move on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Mile Vjeljovic, I believe he died. When we went to Gorazde, I believe that later on he died in Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was he a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I believe he was on the list of the SUP maybe, but I wasn't there when he was taken there, and he couldn't survive. At the beginning, he was with the police, but I'm not sure that he was on their list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Anyone else that you might recognise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Milenko Cosovic, he was also killed at Moremiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, and we would tender this final page of the book of dead into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D 125 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And next, I would ask the Court's assistance in calling up 1D 22-0537.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And after you've had a moment to take a look at the photograph, do you recognise the people that are in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes, I know both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And please describe for the record who the people are and also indicate, because we are on a transcript, who is on the right and who is on the left in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: On the left is Vidoje Andric. He has a bulletproof jacket; and on the right, there's Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And looking at their uniforms, is this consistent with the type of uniforms that members of the reserve police would wear in Visegrad at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And can you make a comment on the patches that are present in the photograph and on the uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I can't see them well, but I could have put any sort of patch on my uniform. Whoever found -- whoever liked something could have put it on their uniform, anything at all. The moment this was blown up, I think I saw that one of the patches said "milicija," but now I'm not sure, speaking about Vidoje. It may have been sewn on his uniform. At the time, the patches said "milicija." He wore this bulletproof jacket all the time, and he had a black belt, and he always worked on his fitness. And the partisan company produced us some plates, up to a centimetre in strength, and he put them in his bulletproof jacket. He always wore it. We even tried to shoot a 7.9-millimetre bullet at it, and it wouldn't -- it couldn't pierce the jacket. It was bulletproof from the front and from behind also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And thank you. Can you comment on the vehicle that they are sitting on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I don't know. I really can't say. It must have been one of the vehicles that were registered for the SUP. Actually, it wasn't a real registration. It was just a sheet of paper. The vehicle may have had regular licence plates, but a document was issued stating that the vehicle was being used by the SUP. It -- this may be a Passat or a Lada. Even Tomic later on drove the better cars, and we would get the worse cars when we were sent to the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, can we pan back on the photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just looking at the surroundings in the neighbourhood, can you tell the Court whereabouts this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: This is -- was taken when -- along the road when you go to -- from Nova Mahala toward the gas station, the Ina [phoen] gas station. That's the first entry to the right. I'm not sure whose houses these exactly are, or, rather, I couldn't tell you for each individual house to who it belongs. There was a warehouse there, a furniture warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, is it true that the Visegrad police used these kind of uniforms at the time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. It's a leading question, and I believe he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is this -- are these uniforms consistent with the kinds that would be worn at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes, they are. I also had one just like this, maybe two. Later on, I would have as many as four or five because uniforms get dirty, so you change because when you return from action, you are all dirty and covered with mud and wet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you comment on the type of weapons that they have in their possession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: These are automatic rifles. I also had one like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's what I was going to ask you. Are these the same or similar that were normally issued to the police at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you couldn't move around without a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just looking at the photograph, they have their arm -- or at least Milan has his arms around Vidoje. How would you characterise Vidoje and Milan's relationship at this time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: They were good friends. They hung out together. They would go to actions together. They would provide a security for Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's been alleged that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: He was the number two man right after Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And there's been evidence led in this case surrounding the name of a group called the White Eagles. Did you have any knowledge of this group known as the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Yes, I do have information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what do you know about the White Eagles in Visegrad at this time in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Both Muslims and Serbs ran from them. Nobody dared oppose them. So it was better to get out of their way. They even took the rifle off my buddy. He didn't dare oppose them. They gave him a better rifle. They took him one of these and gave him one with a wooden butt, and they said, We need one of these with a folding stock, and gave him another. He didn't dare say no because he was afraid of getting killed. So it was better to get out of their way so that you don't run into them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, before I move too far afield, we'd like to introduce the photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection, but we do want to note for the record that this photograph was disclosed just -- very late, was disclosed to us just recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sartorio. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D 126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I don't know if the transcription made it -- or that -- but my counsel -- co-counsel heard that you said they would kill one another, i.e., being the White Eagles. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: I don't know what they were like, whether they used to drink or take drugs, but nobody dared oppose them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Who was the leader?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: They could even take your car and drive it away without you opposing them. You couldn't oppose them; otherwise, you would get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And who was the reputed commander of these people known as the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: There was talk of a guy called Charlie. I don't know who that was, probably an ex-officer of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And where were these people known as the White Eagles housed in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: For a while at Banja and at the Visegrad hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at any time during your being a member of the reserve police force, did the White Eagles ever operate jointly with the Visegrad police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: May we go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when is it the first time that you actually got to know Milan Lukic on a better basis than just being an acquaintance?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at any time later, did you get to know him better than that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Well, I did meet him. I had -- used to have a drink in his cafe, in his inn.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat. We lost the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, please repeat what you just said. The interpreter didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question was how I met him. I got to know him better later. I was at his inn, and we would meet on the street, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court about Risto Perisic's role in Visegrad in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: Risto Perisic was a chief of the SUP. He was the number one man, and right below him there was Tomic. He was number two.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your direct testimony, you mentioned that Vidoje Andric was mobilised before the war. What did you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: It was not before the war. How could it be before the war?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you because at page 32, line 4, that's what you said. So if you could clarify what you meant, that would be helpful. When was he mobilised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD23
utterances.text: The same time as I, maybe a few days before. He left town together with Dragan Tomic to Panos when the Uzice Corps arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, when you refer to mobilisation, I guess I'm confused. Is one mobilised into the army, into the VRS and then assigned to the police, or is one mobilised and seconded? Can you please explain to us what it means to be mobilised and then to end up being a member of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would object only for clarification purposes as the last two lines of the witness's answer were not placed into the transcript. I defer to my counsel as to -- but otherwise ask the witness to repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
